services.name: Shop visit management
services.oneLiner: Full or overview management of an engine shop visit, from pre-induction to redelivery, with every workscope line, finding and invoice item checked independently.
services.metaDescription: Independent engine shop visit management: workscope review, table inspection, test-cell overview and invoice review. On site worldwide from Zug, Switzerland.

problem.title: A purchase most teams make a few times
problem.text: An engine needs three to five shop visits in its life. A performance restoration typically costs several million US dollars, and CFM56 repair costs have risen 50 to 75 per cent since 2019. The shop writes the workscope and the invoice. Someone on your side has to read both and be there when the engine is on the table.

deliverables.title: Full shop visit management
deliverables.text: We run the visit end to end: pre-induction review, workscope, table inspection, repair and material approvals, test cell, invoice and records. Your team gets one file and one point of contact.

deliverables.title: Overview shop visit management
deliverables.text: Your team runs the visit. We review the workscope, attend the table inspection and check the invoice at the points where money is committed.

deliverables.title: Workscope compilation and review
deliverables.text: A preliminary workscope drafted against the planning guide, the lease and the LLP stubs before induction, then the shop's proposal compared with it line by line.

deliverables.title: Dirty condition and table inspection
deliverables.text: Attended in person once the engine is stripped. Findings photographed and recorded, repair or replace decided part by part, before the shop quotes.

deliverables.title: Pre and post repair borescope overview
deliverables.text: Borescope images and video reviewed before induction and after repair, so that the recorded condition and the workscope agree.

deliverables.title: Material sourcing support and documentation audit
deliverables.text: New, used serviceable or repaired parts chosen against lead time, price and records, with the documentation checked before the part goes into the engine.

deliverables.title: Test cell overview
deliverables.text: Test-cell results reviewed against the acceptance limits and the agreed margins, with any shortfall raised before the engine is released.

deliverables.title: Engine overhaul and repair invoice review
deliverables.text: The invoice reconciled against the agreed workscope, the recorded findings and the contract rates. Items outside the agreement are queried before payment.

deliverables.title: Scrap review and material value extraction
deliverables.text: Scrapped parts reviewed against the scrap criteria. Parts with remaining value or a repair option are identified and retained for you.

deliverables.title: Post-shop visit documentation audit and warranty management

engagement.title: Pre-induction
engagement.text: Removal reason, technical status, records and LLP status reviewed. Slot, transport and a preliminary workscope agreed with the shop before the engine arrives.

engagement.title: Table inspection
engagement.text: We attend the dirty condition and table inspection, photograph and record every finding, and settle repair or replace part by part.

engagement.title: Workscope approval
engagement.text: The final workscope is agreed in writing against the findings, the planning guide and the lease. Only what the engine needs is released for repair.

engagement.title: Test cell
engagement.text: Repairs and material are approved as they arise. At the test cell we review the results against the acceptance limits before release.

engagement.title: Invoice reconciliation
engagement.text: The invoice is reconciled against the agreed workscope, the findings and the contract rates. Queries are settled before payment.

engagement.title: Warranty and records
engagement.text: Post-shop visit documentation is audited, warranty items are logged and followed up. The engine is redelivered with a records pack ready for the next event.

proof.title: Every decision on paper
proof.text: Each workscope line, finding and invoice item is recorded in one file that stays with you. Flight Hour Solution is owned by its managing director, not by an MRO, a lessor or an OEM, so on advisory work the only interest at the table is yours.

faq.q: What is the difference between full and overview shop visit management?
faq.a: Full management means we run the visit end to end and are your single point of contact with the shop. Overview management means your own team runs the visit and we review the workscope, attend the table inspection and check the invoice.

faq.q: When should we bring you in?
faq.a: Before the workscope is agreed with the shop, ideally at removal planning. We can join at the table inspection or at the invoice, but the largest decisions are made in the workscope.

faq.q: Do you attend the table inspection in person?
faq.a: Yes. Table inspections, test-cell runs and redeliveries are attended on site, at the shop, wherever the engine is.

faq.q: Which engines do you manage shop visits for?
faq.a: CFM56-3, -5 and -7; LEAP-1A, -1B and -1C; V2500-A1, -A5 and -D5; PW4000-94, -100 and -112; Honeywell APU 131-9A, -9B and -9D; and the TPE331, T76 and TFE731.

problem.title: Slots are scarce. Timing is the lever.
problem.text: Turnaround times are up 35 per cent or more on legacy engines and 150 per cent or more on new-generation engines against pre-pandemic levels. Slot waits have stretched by two to three months, up to six in some cases. An engine removed early wastes life; one removed late waits without a slot. The workscope then decides what the visit costs.

engagement.title: Fleet and records review
engagement.text: Engine status, LLP stubs, trend data, lease terms and the current removal plan are collected into one baseline.

engagement.title: Removal plan
engagement.text: Removal windows are set per engine against limits, margins and slot lead times, and agreed with maintenance planning and finance.

engagement.title: Workscope compilation
engagement.text: For each planned removal a workscope is compiled from the planning guide, the records and the lease, with the target build standard stated.

engagement.title: Shop proposal review
engagement.text: The shop's proposal is compared with the compiled workscope. Differences are settled in writing before induction.

engagement.title: Forecast and handover
engagement.text: Cost forecasts are updated with the agreed scopes. The plan is handed to shop visit management or to your own team for execution.

proof.title: Assumptions you can audit
proof.text: Every forecast and workscope carries its assumptions in writing: utilisation, LLP limits, margin trends, rates and lead times, so your team can challenge them. Nothing is tied to a vendor's tool or to an MRO's capacity.

faq.q: When is the right time to remove an engine?
faq.a: When the remaining LLP life, the EGT margin trend and the slot lead time meet. We set the window per engine from those inputs and the fleet plan, and revisit it as the trends move.

faq.q: What is in a workscope?
faq.a: The inspection and repair level for each module, the LLPs to be replaced, the modifications to be embodied and the build standard the engine must meet on test. It is written against the OEM workscope planning guide and, for leased engines, the lease conditions.

faq.q: Can you help decide whether to embody a durability kit?
faq.a: Yes. For LEAP engines we set the embodiment decision against the engine's expected time on wing, the LLP plan and the cost of the next visit, and record the reasoning.

faq.q: Do you guarantee a shop slot?
faq.a: No. We do not control shop capacity. We plan removals against the lead times shops are quoting and support the negotiation of slots and turnaround commitments.

problem.title: Reserves and redelivery decide who pays
problem.text: Maintenance reserve clauses and redelivery conditions are the two lease provisions most likely to end in a multi-million-dollar dispute, over LLP valuations, deferred defects, incomplete back-to-birth records and the limits of fair wear and tear. With 17,000 aircraft ordered but undelivered, legacy fleets keep flying, and older lease language did not anticipate early shop visits or module swaps.

deliverables.title: Redelivery management for lessees
deliverables.text: The lease's return conditions turned into a work plan months ahead: final shop visit, LLP status, records and the reserve position, worked through before the redelivery inspection rather than during it.

deliverables.title: Redelivery acceptance for lessors
deliverables.text: Technical and records inspection of the returning engine against the lease, with a findings list, a cost estimate for each shortfall and the basis for any claim.

deliverables.title: Reserve claim analysis

deliverables.title: LLP back-to-birth trace audit
deliverables.text: Every life-limited part traced from manufacture to today through the records, with gaps listed and the options to close them assessed.

deliverables.title: Technical documentation audit
deliverables.text: The engine's records package audited against the lease's return standard and airworthiness requirements, ahead of a transition or a sale.

deliverables.title: Post-shop visit documentation audit

deliverables.title: Lessor portfolio support programmes

engagement.title: Lease review
engagement.text: Return conditions, reserve clauses, LLP requirements and the records standard are extracted from the lease into a checklist with dates.

engagement.title: Gap analysis
engagement.text: The engine's current status and records are compared with the checklist. Each gap gets a cost, an owner and a deadline.

engagement.title: Final shop visit
engagement.text: Where a visit is needed to meet the return condition, its workscope is set against the lease and the visit is managed or overseen to the same standard as any other.

engagement.title: Reserve reconciliation
engagement.text: Reserve balances, claims and end-of-lease compensation are calculated from the agreed status and supported line by line.

engagement.title: Redelivery
engagement.text: The redelivery inspection and records handover are attended. Findings are settled on the day where possible, and open items are documented with their value.

proof.title: Either side, or between them
proof.text: We work for the lessee, for the lessor, or as the technical party both accept. Flight Hour Solution is not owned by a lessor or an MRO, and on advisory work our only interest is the client's. When we broker an engine we say so.

faq.q: Do you work for lessors or for airlines?
faq.a: Both, but never for both sides of the same lease at once. We prepare a return for the lessee, accept one for the lessor, or oversee a lessor's portfolio through the lease.

faq.q: How early should redelivery planning start?
faq.a: Before the last shop visit of the lease is planned. The final workscope, the LLP position and the records take longer to put right than the inspection itself.

faq.q: What are the most common causes of dispute at redelivery?
faq.a: LLP valuations, deferred defects, incomplete back-to-birth records and the boundary of fair wear and tear, under the maintenance reserve and redelivery clauses. Each can be checked and priced before the return date.

faq.q: Can you calculate or check maintenance reserves?
faq.a: Yes. We model reserve rates and balances against the expected shop visit and LLP cost for each engine, and check claims against those reserves for eligibility and invoice support.

faq.q: Power by the hour or time and material?
faq.a: It depends on utilisation, fleet age, your own engineering capacity and your appetite for cost variance. We model both against the fleet plan and negotiate the terms of whichever fits, including the exit and transfer clauses.

faq.q: Do you negotiate with the MRO directly?
faq.a: As you prefer. We can lead the technical negotiation, sit beside your procurement team, or prepare positions and review drafts in the background.

faq.q: Can you review invoices from shop visits you did not manage?
faq.a: Yes. We reconcile the invoice against the contract rates, the agreed workscope and the shop's own findings report, and give you a written list of queries with their value.

faq.q: Are you tied to any MRO or parts supplier?
faq.a: No. Flight Hour Solution is owned by its managing director, not by an MRO, a lessor or an OEM. Engine and aircraft sourcing is done under a separate Assets line and is always disclosed.

deliverables.text: Support to your engineers on a live problem: which data to pull, what the borescope should look at, whether the engine can stay on wing and under what monitoring.

deliverables.title: Engine on-wing performance review
deliverables.text: EGT margin, fuel flow and vibration trends reviewed per engine, with the remaining margin to a removal set against LLP limits and the fleet plan.

deliverables.title: Borescope overview and video analysis
deliverables.text: Borescope stills and video read against the manual limits and the engine's history, with a written condition statement and a repeat-inspection interval.

deliverables.title: Test cell and on-wing run result analysis
deliverables.text: Test-cell and on-wing run data reviewed against the acceptance limits and the pre-visit condition, so a marginal pass is seen for what it is.

deliverables.title: Removal timing recommendations
deliverables.text: For each monitored engine, the recommended removal window and the reasoning behind it, updated as the trend moves and handed to workscope planning.

deliverables.title: Maintenance cost forecasting from trend data
deliverables.text: Forecasts that use measured margin decay rather than average intervals, so budgets follow the engines you actually operate.

engagement.title: Data access
engagement.text: We agree which sources we read: OEM portal exports, MRO reports, your maintenance system, borescope archives. No new platform is installed.

engagement.title: Baseline
engagement.text: Each engine's trend history, findings and LLP position are reviewed once, and the fleet is ranked by remaining margin.

engagement.title: Monitoring cycle
engagement.text: Trends are reviewed on the agreed cycle. Alerts are interpreted, recommendations issued in writing and discussed with your engineers.

engagement.title: Removal call
engagement.text: When an engine approaches its window, the removal date is recommended with the evidence, and the workscope is drafted from the same data.

engagement.title: Feedback from the shop
engagement.text: Table inspection findings are compared with what the data predicted, and the assumptions are corrected from the evidence.

proof.title: No platform, no shop capacity to sell
proof.text: We do not sell a monitoring platform or shop capacity, so the recommendation is not shaped by what happens after the removal. Every alert we interpret is answered in writing, with the data behind it.

faq.q: Do we need to install new software?
faq.a: No. We work from the data you already have: OEM portal exports, MRO trend reports, your maintenance system and borescope archives.

faq.q: How is this different from the OEM's monitoring service?
faq.a: The OEM's service is built on its own fleet models and its own aftermarket. We read the same data for you alone, and our recommendation is not tied to a repair network.

faq.q: Can you review a single borescope finding?
faq.a: Yes. Send the stills or video and the engine's history, and you get a written condition statement against the manual limits, with a recommended next inspection.

faq.q: Do you cover APUs and turboprops?
faq.a: Yes. Honeywell 131-9A, -9B and -9D APUs, the TPE331 and T76, and the TFE731 are covered with the same trend and test-result review.

problem.title: Value now sits in the engines
problem.text: Lenders scrutinise engine status more closely than before, and an aircraft can no longer be assessed by model, age and lease status alone: one with serviceable engines, strong records and manageable maintenance exposure may be worth more than a similar one facing engine uncertainty. The records, the LLP position and the next shop visit are the valuation.

deliverables.title: Engine evaluation and selection
deliverables.text: Candidate engines compared on technical status, LLP position, records, modification standard and expected cost to the next shop visit, for a purchase, a lease or a fleet decision.

deliverables.title: Technical documentation audit
deliverables.text: The full records package audited: airworthiness release, modification and repair history, AD and SB status, LLP traceability, and the gaps that would stop a sale or a lease.

deliverables.title: LLP back-to-birth trace audit
deliverables.text: Every life-limited part traced from manufacture to the current build through the paperwork. Missing links are listed with the options and the cost to close them.

deliverables.title: Maintenance status and cost forecast
deliverables.text: Time and cycles since the last visit, remaining LLP life and margin, and a forecast of the next shop visit's timing and cost with the assumptions stated.

deliverables.title: Borescope and test result review
deliverables.text: Recent borescope and test-cell data read independently, so the stated condition and the evidence agree before the price is fixed.

deliverables.title: Engine teardown valuation
deliverables.text: What the engine is worth in parts: LLP remaining life, repairable rotables, scrap, and the cost and time of a teardown, as a floor for the price or as an exit option.

deliverables.title: Portfolio engine exposure review
deliverables.text: For a portfolio or an ABS pool: shop visit timing by engine, reserve adequacy, spare coverage and the records position, ranked by exposure.

deliverables.title: Post-shop visit documentation audit
deliverables.text: For an engine fresh from overhaul: release documents, workscope, findings and test data audited against what was paid for.

engagement.title: Scope and access
engagement.text: The transaction, the timetable and the questions to be answered are agreed. Records access is arranged with the seller, lessee or servicer.

engagement.title: Desk review
engagement.text: Records, LLP status, modification standard and maintenance history are audited against the checklist and the transaction documents.

engagement.title: Physical inspection
engagement.text: Where the engine is accessible, a visual and borescope inspection is attended, and the physical state is reconciled with the paperwork.

engagement.title: Forecast and valuation
engagement.text: Next shop visit timing and cost, the reserve or compensation position and, where required, the teardown value are modelled with stated assumptions.

engagement.title: Report
engagement.text: A written report with findings ranked by value at risk, the open items and how to close them, delivered before the decision date and defended in your meetings.

proof.title: Written for the decision
proof.text: Reports rank findings by value at risk and state every assumption, so a credit committee or an investment board can test them. Flight Hour Solution is not owned by a lessor, an MRO or an OEM. When we broker an asset we say so.

faq.q: What do you need from the seller or lessee?
faq.a: The records package, the current status report, LLP status, the last shop visit report and test data, and access to the engine for a visual and borescope inspection where possible. We send a checklist at the start.

faq.q: Do you provide certified appraisals?
faq.a: We provide technical due diligence, maintenance status forecasts and teardown valuations. Where a transaction requires an appraisal certified under a specific standard, we work alongside the appointed appraiser.

faq.q: Can you assess an engine we cannot inspect physically?
faq.a: Yes, from the records and recent borescope and test data, with the limits of a desk review stated in the report.

faq.q: Do you review whole portfolios?
faq.a: Yes. For a portfolio or an ABS pool we rank each engine by shop visit timing, reserve adequacy, spare coverage and records position, so the exposure is visible at a glance.

problem.title: Readiness with the OEM as sole supplier
problem.text: The global military aircraft fleet is set to grow from 44,700 in 2025 to 50,700 by 2036, with military MRO growing about ten times faster than in the previous decade, led by engine maintenance. Government operators often face a single supplier for engine overhaul, with limited visibility of workscope, cost and turnaround. Someone on the programme's side has to read both.

proof.text: Flight Hour Solution is a privately owned Swiss company, not owned by an OEM, an MRO or a lessor, and not part of any national industrial group. Confidentiality terms are agreed before any programme data is shared.

faq.q: Do you hold security clearances?
faq.a: Security requirements are agreed programme by programme. Tell us the classification of the material involved and we will confirm what we can do and under which arrangements.

faq.q: Which engine types do you cover for government fleets?

faq.q: Can you work within public procurement rules?
faq.a: Our role is technical adviser to the programme office. Independence, scope and confidentiality are documented so that the arrangement fits the procurement file.

faq.q: Where is Flight Hour Solution based, and where do you work?
faq.a: In Zug, Switzerland. Work is on site at the depot, the OEM's shop or the operator's base, wherever the engine is.

problem.title: Experience is leaving faster than it arrives
problem.text: A new technician needs two to five years to reach full productivity, and in the United States 41 per cent of certified mechanics are over 60, with 45,000 expected to retire within a decade. Reading a workscope or an invoice is learned on the job. Knowledge transfer keeps that judgement inside your team rather than inside the shop's.

faq.q: Who is the training for?
faq.a: Powerplant and maintenance planning teams, procurement and contracts staff, technical asset managers at lessors, and programme staff in government fleets. Content is adjusted to the role.

faq.q: Is the training certified or accredited?
faq.a: No. It is practical, method-based training from a working consultancy, not an approved course under a regulatory training standard.

faq.q: Can training be combined with a real shop visit?
faq.a: Yes. Knowledge transfer during a managed shop visit or lease return is the most direct format: your engineers work alongside us and keep the method afterwards.

faq.a: CFM56, LEAP, V2500, PW4000, Honeywell APU 131-9A, -9B and -9D, and the TPE331, T76 and TFE731, with examples drawn from the family your fleet operates.
